title: Types of management information systems
blurb: Information systems, TPS, MIS, the other systems and expert systems.

topics.name: Information systems
topics.line: Data goes in, processing happens, information comes out.
topics.remember: Data, then Processing, then Information (never the other way round). IS is wider than IT. Everything outside the system boundary is the environment.
topics.simple: A shop turns materials into goods. A business turns data into information the same way. The whole set of systems and procedures that does this is the information system. The computers and equipment are only the IT part of it.
frames: Input: raw data goes in, such as marks and attendance.
Processing: the data becomes totals, percentages and grades.
Output: useful information comes out, such as report cards.
The boundary marks the system. Students, teachers and parents outside it are the environment.
gls: a set of interacting components working together for a purpose
all systems and procedures for collecting, storing, producing and distributing information
the equipment used to capture, store, send or show information
planning, organising, controlling and using information and systems to support business aims

cards.mean: A set of interacting components that operate together to accomplish a purpose
cards.ex: A school with teachers, rooms, timetable and rules.

cards.mean: A collection of people, machines and methods organised to do specific functions
cards.ex: A shop: the owner, the billing machine and the way bills are made.

cards.mean: All systems and procedures to collect, store, produce and distribute information. Includes hardcopy as well as electronic flows
cards.ex: Collecting marks, storing them, making report cards, giving them to parents.

cards.mean: The equipment used to capture, store, transmit or present information. IT is a large part of the IS infrastructure
cards.ex: The computers, scanners and networks of the school.

cards.mean: Planning, organising, controlling and using information and systems to support business aims
cards.ex: Deciding what information is needed, which technology, how to protect it and how to improve it.

cards.mean: Raw data fed into the system. It can also be the output of another system
cards.ex: Student names, roll numbers, marks, attendance.

cards.mean: Turns data into useful information. There may not be a 1 to 1 link between inputs and outputs
cards.ex: Totals, percentages, grades, rankings, pass or fail.

cards.mean: The final useful result given back to users
cards.ex: Report cards, grade sheets, class rankings.

cards.mean: The border that separates the system from its environment
cards.ex: Result software, database, grading rules and report modules are inside.

cards.mean: Everything outside the boundary. It gives inputs and receives outputs, and can influence the system
cards.ex: Students, teachers, parents, school office, education board.

items.q: Marks and roll numbers entered for each student
items.why: Raw data going in is input.

items.q: Calculating total marks, percentages and grades
items.why: Turning data into information is processing.

items.q: Report cards printed for each student
items.why: The useful result is output.

items.q: The grading rules and the result database
items.why: Everything that helps process the results is inside the boundary.

items.q: Parents who receive the report cards
items.why: People outside the boundary who receive outputs are the environment.

caps: Input: raw data enters the system, such as marks and attendance.
Processing turns data into information: totals, percentages, grades.
Output: useful information leaves, such as report cards.
The system boundary separates the system from its environment.
Everything outside the boundary is the environment. It gives inputs and receives outputs.

topics.name: Transaction processing system
topics.line: Records the routine, repetitive transactions of daily business.
topics.remember: TPS performs, records and processes routine transactions. It is used in Marketing, Production, Finance and HR, and it is the foundation data source for the MIS.
topics.simple: Every sale, purchase, invoice and salary payment is a routine transaction. The TPS is the system that records them all, day after day, in large numbers. Other systems later use this data.
frames: A sale is made and the sales order is recorded.
Purchases and production steps are recorded.
Invoices and ledger entries are recorded.
Payroll and employee records are recorded.
gls: a system that performs, records and processes routine transactions
materials resource planning, managing raw materials

cards.mean: Handles the normal tasks that happen again and again
cards.ex: Recording every sale at a counter.

cards.mean: Processes a very large number of transactions
cards.ex: Thousands of bills in a month.

cards.mean: Supports the day-to-day running of the business
cards.ex: Payroll run each month.

cards.mean: Provides data for systems such as the MIS
cards.ex: Sales data becomes a sales report.

cards.mean: Used in almost every part of the business
cards.ex: Sales, production, finance and HR.

cards.mean: Sales management, marketing research, promotion pricing, new products
cards.ex: Sales order system, marketing research system, pricing system.

cards.mean: Scheduling, purchasing, shipping and receiving, engineering, operations
cards.ex: MRP, purchase order control, engineering system, quality control system.

cards.mean: Budgeting, nominal ledger, invoicing, management accounting
cards.ex: Nominal ledger, accounts receivable and payable, budgeting, treasury management.

cards.mean: Personnel records, benefits, salaries, labour relations, training
cards.ex: Payroll, employee records, employee benefits, career path system.

items.q: Sales order system
items.why: It records customer orders, so it belongs to sales.

items.q: Quality control system
items.why: It checks product quality in production.

items.q: Nominal ledger system
items.why: It records all financial transactions.

items.q: Payroll system
items.why: It calculates and pays salaries.

items.q: Pricing system
items.why: It sets and updates product prices.

items.q: Purchase order control
items.why: It creates and tracks purchase orders for raw materials.

items.q: Treasury management system
items.why: It manages cash and funds.

items.q: Career path system
items.why: It tracks promotions and growth of staff.

items.q: Materials resource planning (MRP)
items.why: MRP manages raw materials for production.

items.q: Employee benefits system
items.why: It manages perks and benefits.

caps: A TPS performs, records and processes routine transactions.
Sales and marketing: sales orders, pricing, market research.
Production: purchase orders, materials planning, quality control.
Finance and accounting: ledgers, invoices, budgets.
Human resources: payroll, employee records, benefits.
The TPS data feeds other systems, such as the MIS.

topics.name: Management information system
topics.line: Turns TPS data into summary and exception reports for managers.
topics.remember: MIS = mainly internal data from the TPS, summarised into regular reports for routine, structured decisions. Limited analysis and fixed formats. TPS is the foundation of MIS.
topics.simple: The TPS records every single sale. A manager does not want thousands of lines. The MIS adds them up into one short report, and warns when something is wrong. The manager then makes an everyday decision.
frames: The MIS adds them into a summary report.
It also raises an exception report when something is off.
The manager makes a routine decision using the report.
gls: converts mainly internal data into summary and exception reports for managers
only the items that are unusual or off target

cards.mean: Helps managers make routine, well-defined decisions
cards.ex: Reordering stock when it falls to a set level.

cards.mean: Focuses on day-to-day activities
cards.ex: Today's sales and stock.

cards.mean: Scheduled summary and exception reports
cards.ex: A weekly sales report.

cards.mean: Does not do deep or complex analysis
cards.ex: It reports totals, it does not model what-if cases.

cards.mean: Fixed report formats and structures
cards.ex: The same report layout every week.

cards.mean: Mainly uses data from inside the organisation
cards.ex: Its own sales and cost data.

items.q: Records each sale as it happens
items.why: Recording routine transactions is the TPS.

items.q: A weekly sales summary by branch
items.why: Summarised reports for managers are the MIS.

items.q: An exception report on overdue invoices
items.why: Exception reports come from the MIS.

items.q: Processes a very large number of routine transactions
items.why: That is the TPS.

items.q: Uses fixed report formats with limited analysis
items.why: That describes an MIS.

items.q: The data source the MIS is built on
items.why: The TPS is the foundation of the MIS.

caps: The TPS records every transaction, such as each sale.
The MIS adds that data into a regular summary report.
It also flags exceptions, such as stock below the minimum.
Managers use the reports for routine, structured decisions.
MIS uses internal data from the TPS, fixed formats and limited analysis.

topics.name: Other information systems
topics.line: ESS, DSS, KWS, OAS, ERP and CRM, each with a different job.
topics.remember: ESS/EIS: senior managers, strategic. DSS: data plus analytical models. KWS: create and share new knowledge. OAS: productivity of data and information workers. ERP: integrates core processes. CRM: customers.
topics.simple: A big organisation needs more than reports. Executives need a dashboard. Managers need to test choices. IT teams create new knowledge. Office staff need email and spreadsheets. The ERP joins all departments. The CRM looks after customers.
frames: ESS/EIS: a dashboard for senior managers.
DSS: data plus models to choose between options.
KWS: helps create and share new knowledge.
OAS: email, documents and spreadsheets for office staff.
gls: presents internal and external data for senior managers
data plus analytical models for semi-structured and unstructured decisions
helps create, develop and share new knowledge
raises productivity of data and information workers
one integrated system for HR, finance, inventory and operations
manages relationships with existing and potential customers

cards.mean: Collects internal and external data and shows it in an easy form for senior managers. Helps strategic, unstructured decisions
cards.ex: Bank executives use dashboards of profit, deposits and loans to decide on expansion.

cards.mean: Combines data with analytical models and tools for semi-structured and unstructured decisions
cards.ex: Managers analyse loan risk and credit before approving or rejecting a loan.

cards.mean: Helps create, develop and share new knowledge in the organisation
cards.ex: The bank IT team develops new banking apps.

cards.mean: Increases the productivity of data and information workers with email, documents and spreadsheets
cards.ex: Staff use email, Excel and Word for reports.

cards.mean: An integrated system for core processes such as HR, finance, inventory and operations
cards.ex: One system connects all bank departments.

cards.mean: Manages relationships with existing and potential customers to improve service and sales
cards.ex: Tracks customer accounts and loans to make offers.

cards.mean: Hospital managers use bed availability, cost and patient trends for big planning decisions
cards.ex: Deciding on a new hospital service or expansion.

cards.mean: Ward managers use reports on patients, costs and resources to run the ward within budget
cards.ex: Managing staff and beds daily.

cards.mean: Doctors use lab results, scans and data to choose treatments
cards.ex: Selecting the best medicine or procedure.

cards.mean: Phone or online systems ask symptoms and suggest possible diagnoses
cards.ex: A medical helpline triage system.

cards.mean: Doctors and nurses share case notes and discuss cases by video
cards.ex: Consulting specialists in other hospitals.

cards.mean: Appointments, reports, emails and hospital communication
cards.ex: Booking and scheduling patients.

cards.mean: Daily operations such as pharmacy orders and dispensing
cards.ex: Recording medicine issued to patients.

cards.mean: Connects patient records, staff, pharmacy and supplies
cards.ex: One system for the whole hospital.

cards.mean: Manages patient records, visits and follow-ups
cards.ex: Reminders for check-ups.

items.q: Bank executives view a dashboard of profit, deposits and loans
items.why: A dashboard for senior managers is an ESS/EIS.

items.q: Managers analyse loan risk before approving a loan
items.why: Data plus analysis to choose between options is a DSS.

items.q: The IT team develops a new banking app
items.why: Creating new knowledge and solutions is the KWS role.

items.q: Staff use email, Excel and Word for daily reports
items.why: Everyday office tools are an OAS.

items.q: One system connects HR, accounts, transactions and operations
items.why: Integrating core processes is ERP.

items.q: Tracking customer accounts to send better offers
items.why: Managing customer relationships is CRM.

o.s: Executives view profit and loan dashboards
Managers weigh loan risk, approve or reject
The IT team builds new banking apps
Staff use email, Excel and Word

caps: ESS/EIS: senior managers see internal and external data for strategic, unstructured decisions.
DSS: data plus analytical models for semi-structured and unstructured decisions.
KWS: helps create, develop and share new knowledge.
OAS: raises the productivity of data and information workers.
ERP: one integrated system for HR, finance, inventory and operations.
CRM: manages relationships with existing and potential customers.

topics.name: Expert systems
topics.line: A knowledge base plus an inference engine gives expert advice to non-experts.
topics.remember: Expert system = Knowledge base (the rules) + Inference engine (applies the rules to the user's facts). It suggests, it does not replace humans. Main reason for use: relative cost.
topics.simple: An expert system is like a helper who has read every rule an expert knows. You tell it the facts of your case, it applies the rules and suggests an answer. A bank can approve a small loan over the phone without a manager.
frames: The knowledge base stores the expert's rules and facts.
The user enters the facts of the case.
The inference engine applies the rules to those facts.
It suggests a conclusion, like a decision-making assistant.
gls: the expert's decision rules, facts and domain knowledge
applies the rules to the user's facts to reach a conclusion
the one subject area the system covers

cards.mean: Contains the expert's decision-making rules, facts and specialised knowledge about the domain
cards.ex: Lending rules of a bank.

cards.mean: Applies the rules to the circumstances entered by the user to reach a conclusion or suggestion
cards.ex: Checks a loan applicant against the rules.

cards.mean: Works like a decision-making assistant. It suggests, it does not replace humans
cards.ex: A loan officer still takes responsibility.

cards.mean: The problem is reasonably well defined, cannot be solved by normal transaction processing, and experts are highly paid
cards.ex: Credit decisions with clear rules.

cards.mean: Applies stored legal or tax rules to user data to suggest possible outcomes
cards.ex: Likely tax result of a transaction.

cards.mean: Analyses past data with pattern rules to predict trends
cards.ex: Inflation or demand.

cards.mean: Compares real-time data with set limits and rules
cards.ex: Monitoring stock levels.

cards.mean: Matches symptoms or error signals with known fault patterns
cards.ex: A machine fault or a medical condition.

cards.mean: Uses rules to adjust timelines from progress and constraints
cards.ex: Resolving schedule delays.

cards.mean: Compares student answers with model answers to find weak areas
cards.ex: Suggesting improvements.

cards.mean: A human expert costs more to employ or hire. A system is built once and serves many users
cards.ex: One system, many branches.

cards.mean: Expert wisdom reaches more people, so less experienced staff can decide
cards.ex: A junior uses senior rules.

cards.mean: Years of knowledge are available at once
cards.ex: A repair engineer's plant knowledge.

cards.mean: Has knowledge and limited reasoning, so decisions are faster
cards.ex: Quick loan answers.

cards.mean: Applies the rules the same way every time
cards.ex: No variation between experts.

items.q: Holds the expert's decision rules
items.why: The rules and facts are the knowledge base.

items.q: Applies the rules to the user's facts
items.why: Applying rules to a case is the inference engine.

items.q: Stores specialised knowledge about the domain
items.why: Stored knowledge is the knowledge base.

items.q: Reaches a conclusion or suggestion
items.why: The engine produces the conclusion.

o.s: enters the facts: credit record, income, security
applies the rules to the facts

caps: The knowledge base holds the expert's rules, facts and know-how.
The user enters the facts of a case, such as a loan applicant.
The inference engine applies the rules to those facts.
It suggests a conclusion, like a decision-making assistant.
Used for legal and tax advice, forecasting, surveillance, diagnosis, projects and training.
